div.head: III Eg 2.1
div.ab: Gyf þæt riht to hefig sy, sece siþþan ða lihtinge to þam cynge.
Gyf þæt riht to hefig sy, sece syððan þa lyhtinge to þam cynge.
Gif þæt riht to hefig sy, secan siððan þa lihtinge to ðam cynge.
Si rectum graue nimis est, postea querat inde ueniam apud regem.
Gif þæt riht to hefig sy, secan siððan þa lihtinge to ðam cynge.
Gyf þæt riht to hefig sy, sece siþþan ða lihtinge to þam cynge.
Wenn das [Land]recht zu streng ist, heische er (-en sie D) dann die Erleichterung vom König.
If the [law of the land] is too severe, let him (them, D) then seek relief from the king.
If the law is too oppressive, he shall apply to the king for mitigation.
If that law is too severe, he is then to apply to the king for alleviation.
If the law is too harsh, let him petition the king for mitigation.

note.seg: Vgl. Gl Billigkeit 2b—4. Eine unbeschränkte Dispensationsbefugnis des Königs sieht hierin v. Amira Grundriss³ 155, wohl zu weitgehend. Vgl. Vinogradoff Early hist. of Engl. Equity (in Essays in legal hist., Internat. congr. 1913) 261

Cf. Gl Billigkeit 2b—4. v. Amira, Grundriss³ 155, sees in this an unlimited power of dispensation on the king’s part, probably going too far. Cf. Vinogradoff Early hist. of Engl. Equity (in Essays in legal hist., Internat. congr. 1913) 261

See Brunner, ii. p. 136, for references to similar mitigation in continental codes of law. Liebermann is of opinion that in England this right probably rested, not with the king alone, but with a special royal court (see ii. p. 313, s.v. Billigkeit, 4, and The National Assembly in the A.S. Period, p. 68), but the evidence for such a court in the tenth century seems to be far from conclusive.
